items.title: iCAUR 03T Electric SUV Arrives
items.summary: iCAUR South Africa has officially launched the 03T electric SUV, bringing a new contender to the country's expanding new-energy vehicle market. The model, positioned above the brand's existing V23 in the local lineup, goes on…
items.content_html:
iCAUR South Africa has officially launched the 03T electric SUV, bringing a new contender to the country's expanding new-energy vehicle market. The model, positioned above the brand's existing V23 in the local lineup, goes on sale in South African showrooms from 28 May 2026 and is priced from R639,900.

The 03T is the latest offering from iCAUR, the new-energy sub-brand operating under the Chery Global umbrella. It arrives in two derivatives — a rear-wheel-drive 2WD and an all-wheel-drive AWD — giving buyers a choice between efficient single-motor performance and more capable dual-motor output.

The 2WD variant is powered by a single rear-mounted electric motor producing 135 kW and 220 N.m of torque, drawing from a 65.69 kWh battery. It accelerates from 0 to 100 km/h in 10.5 seconds and returns an NEDC-estimated range of 431 km at a consumption rate of 18.3 kWh/100 km.

The AWD derivative pairs a dual-motor setup for a combined output of 205 kW and 385 N.m, supported by a slightly larger 69.77 kWh battery. It covers the 0 to 100 km/h sprint in 6.5 seconds and offers an NEDC-estimated range of 436 km at 19.9 kWh/100 km. Both variants are limited to a top speed of 150 km/h and can be charged from 10% to 80% via DC fast charging in 30 minutes.

Bold Proportions and a Well-Appointed Cabin

Visually, the 03T adopts a squared-off, upright stance with pronounced wheel arches and slim LED lighting elements. Its all-aluminium multi-cavity cage body is engineered for corrosion resistance of up to 30 years, while reducing vehicle weight by more than 30% and lowering energy consumption by 3%.

A panoramic glass sunroof and 19-inch alloy wheels wrapped in 245/55 tyres complete the exterior. Five paint options are available, spanning Khaki White, Carbon Crystal Black, Cyan Grey, Starlight Silver, and Toronto Red.

Inside, the 03T seats five across a 2,715 mm wheelbase, with 450 litres of boot space that expands to 1,238 litres with the 60:40 split-folding rear seats lowered. A rear storage box adds a further 40 litres.

Both trims feature a 15.6-inch touchscreen, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, voice command functionality, a 540-degree surround-view camera, and a 50-watt wireless charger. The 2WD is fitted with an eight-speaker audio system, while the AWD upgrades to a 12-speaker Infinity setup.

Seat specification on the 2WD includes black leather upholstery, climate control, ambient lighting, and electrically adjustable heated and ventilated front seats with four-way lumbar support. AWD buyers gain a massage function for front occupants and an electrically adjustable passenger leg rest.

Safety and Ownership Support

The 03T carries six airbags across both trims, alongside a full suite of active driver assistance systems. These include Automatic Emergency Braking with vehicle, pedestrian and bicycle recognition, Adaptive Cruise Control, Lane Departure Warning and Prevention, Blind Spot Detection, and Traffic Jam Assist, among others. Front and rear parking sensors and ISOFIX anchorage points are standard throughout the range.

Shannon Gahagan, National Brand and Marketing Manager at iCAUR South Africa, described the 03T as a clear expression of the brand's identity. "Its design gives it a distinctive presence, but the real strength of the 03T is how it combines that personality with comfort, space, safety, and a choice of electric drivetrains suited to different customer needs," she said.

Both models are backed by an eight-year/200,000 km vehicle warranty, an eight-year/160,000 km power battery warranty for the first owner, a five-year/100,000 km service plan, and eight-year/200,000 km roadside assistance. The 2WD is priced at R639,900 and the AWD at R699,900.

items.title: Hino adds hybrid trucks to Kinto
items.summary: Hino South Africa has launched a limited batch of diesel-electric hybrid trucks locally, with the first vehicles already entering service through Namlog at the Toyota Africa Parts Centre in Ekurhuleni. The company says it is…
items.content_html:
Hino South Africa has launched a limited batch of diesel-electric hybrid trucks locally, with the first vehicles already entering service through Namlog at the Toyota Africa Parts Centre in Ekurhuleni.

The company says it is initially importing 32 hybrid models in its 300 Series range, with eight already in the country. Three are currently in operation and a further five will join the fleet soon, while the remaining 24 units will be distributed to major fleet operators.

The trucks will be offered through Toyota’s international Kinto subscription model, which bundles the vehicle, servicing and maintenance into a single monthly payment. Hino says the system is designed to simplify fleet management, while Kinto Protect offers optional comprehensive insurance for fleet operators.

Hino says the 300 Series hybrids have been delivering fuel savings of between 15% and 30%, depending on the type of operation. At a time of high diesel prices and mounting pressure on transport operators to reduce emissions, that could make hybrids an increasingly attractive option for urban and regional delivery fleets.

The launch also highlights a pragmatic route to lower-emission freight transport in South Africa. While battery-electric trucks remain part of the global conversation, diesel-electric hybrids can cut fuel use and carbon emissions without requiring charging infrastructure or major operational changes.

Hino says the hybrid rollout forms part of its broader multi-pathway energy strategy. The company has also revealed that a prototype dual-fuel truck using diesel and hydrogen will be previewed in South Africa next month.

items.title: Bolt EV fleet comes to Cape Town
items.summary: Bolt has struck a partnership with China’s Dongfeng Motor Group to introduce electric vehicles on its ride hailing platform, starting with a fleet in Cape Town. The deal brings Dongfeng’s Box hatchback and a higher…
items.content_html:
Bolt has struck a partnership with China’s Dongfeng Motor Group to introduce electric vehicles on its ride hailing platform, starting with a fleet in Cape Town.

The deal brings Dongfeng’s Box hatchback and a higher spec 007 sedan to Bolt riders, with fleet operations handled by Yugo Rides. Bolt says the move is aimed at improving ride economics for drivers as fuel prices rise and operating costs remain a pressure point.

Simo Kalajdzic, who oversees Bolt’s South African operations, said the country sits at the centre of the firm’s local expansion plans. “With the investment we are making, and the platform we are building, South Africa remains a strong strategic priority for us.”

Cape Town pilot and fleet models

Cape Town has been selected as the first launch market because charging options are more developed there than in many other South African cities, and because the company plans to roll out the vehicles in stages.

“We are taking a phased approach to launching this fleet as we consider the current infrastructure limitations, including the need for enough charging stations,” Kalajdzic said.

Kalajdzic added that the company has invested about $180 million in the South African market and claims more than half of the country’s ride hailing business. That scale gives Bolt a test bed for new vehicle programmes and a route to place electric cars into high mileage service.

For Dongfeng, the partnership offers a visible entry point in a market where Chinese carmakers are increasing exports. The arrangement also puts unfamiliar models in front of riders.

Costs, charging and long term strategy

Electric vehicles can reduce day to day running costs for ride hailing drivers, particularly when petrol and diesel prices move higher. The impact of the Iran war on oil prices has added urgency for ride-sharing platforms that rely on drivers absorbing fuel costs.

However, public charging infrastructure remains limited outside major hubs, and grid constraints have shaped energy planning for businesses. Bolt’s staged approach suggests a focus on operational reliability, with fleet management designed to simplify charging, maintenance, and vehicle availability.

The announcement also lands as Bolt weighs longer term capital markets options. The company, backed by Sequoia Capital, has expanded across more than 50 countries and 850 cities and previously raised €628 million in a 2022 funding round that valued it at €7.4 billion.

Kalajdzic said Bolt “will consider options, when market conditions are right,” a comment likely to keep speculation about an initial public offering in focus. Bolt runs food delivery and scooters and says South Africa sits among its ten biggest markets worldwide.

Industry analysts will watch the Cape Town rollout for evidence that electric fleets can scale in South Africa. If utilisation rates hold and charging downtime stays low, the model could support expansion to other cities and offer a template for similar launches across the continent.

items.title: SA's electric vehicle market edges forward
items.summary: South Africa sold 16,716 new energy vehicles in 2025, a 7.1% increase from 15,611 units the previous year, according to figures released at the official launch of the 2026 naamsa Automotive Trade Manual. The result,…
items.content_html:
South Africa sold 16,716 new energy vehicles in 2025, a 7.1% increase from 15,611 units the previous year, according to figures released at the official launch of the 2026 naamsa Automotive Trade Manual.

The result, representing a 2.8% share of total new vehicle sales of 597,338 units, points to steady if modest progress in a market where price remains the dominant obstacle to faster adoption.

Of the 16,716 new energy vehicles sold, 7,088 were battery electric vehicles, with the remainder comprising hybrids and plug-in hybrids. Naamsa uses the term "new energy vehicle" to capture the full spectrum of electrified drivetrains, and the data in the manual breaks these down across all three categories.

The distinction matters in a market where hybrids are outperforming their fully electric counterparts by a considerable margin, largely because consumers are more willing to absorb a modest price premium than a substantial one.

"On average globally, the price differential between a battery electric and an equivalent internal combustion engine vehicle is 52%, on a plug-in hybrid 43%, and a hybrid 12%," said Dr Norman Lamprecht, naamsa's head of trade and research. "Hybrids are doing well because consumers are willing to pay around 10% for new technology."

South Africa's new vehicle market offers consumers an exceptionally wide range of choice, with 56 passenger car brands and 1,995 model derivatives available in 2025, described at the launch as the greatest selection relative to market size found anywhere globally.

That breadth of choice, combined with lower interest rates and subdued vehicle price inflation, drove overall new vehicle sales up 15.7% during the year. The electric vehicle segment, by comparison, grew at less than half that rate, underscoring the affordability challenge that naamsa says requires a direct policy response.

Demand-side support central to transition debate

naamsa has consistently argued that the transition to electric vehicles requires both production incentives and consumer subsidies, and that position was restated firmly at the launch.

The association pointed to global precedent, noting that electric vehicle sales worldwide surged 21% in 2025, with China accounting for 71% of all electric vehicles sold globally. That dominance, naamsa noted, has been built on sustained and substantial demand-side stimulus.

"All around the world, sales are supported by demand-side stimulus," said Lamprecht. "Considering that affordability is driving new vehicle sales in South Africa already relating to internal combustion engine vehicles, the prices of plug-ins and battery electrics are still fairly high, which is a stumbling block."

The question of demand-side support forms part of the broader review of the Automotive Production and Development Programme currently under way between industry, government, and labour. naamsa president, Peter van Binsbergen confirmed at the launch that the process remained ongoing and that a final position had not yet been reached.

African market and import growth reshape the landscape

The growing availability of lower-priced electric vehicles, many of them from China, is beginning to shift the affordability equation.

Chinese vehicles accounted for 23.3% of all light vehicle imports into South Africa in 2025, up from 17.1% the previous year, with India remaining the top source at 56.2%. Total light vehicle imports grew 28.6% to 391,287 units, reflecting both the expansion of consumer choice and the competitive pressure bearing down on locally assembled models.

Chinese manufacturer Chery, whose Jetour brand is planning local manufacturing operations, was cited at the launch as an example of the investment interest that trade engagement with China could unlock.

naamsa said it was encouraging government to press China to source more from South Africa as part of any reciprocal trade arrangement under the China-Africa Economic Partnership Agreement, which extended duty-free access to 53 African countries from 1 May this year.

On the export side, South Africa's electric vehicle transition carries implications for its African market ambitions as well.

Several African countries are moving towards restrictions on internal combustion engine vehicles, a development naamsa acknowledged while maintaining that export opportunities across the continent remain substantial, particularly following the adoption of automotive rules of origin under the African Continental Free Trade Area in February this year.

items.title: SA's grid problem is also its EV opportunity
items.summary: South Africa sits in an uncomfortable position in Africa's electric vehicle story. According to the Africa E-Mobility Alliance's latest continental signals report, the country's average annual power outage stands at 48.5 hours, the highest among…
items.content_html:
South Africa sits in an uncomfortable position in Africa's electric vehicle story. According to the Africa E-Mobility Alliance's latest continental signals report, the country's average annual power outage stands at 48.5 hours, the highest among the eleven leading African e-mobility markets tracked.

Rwanda, by comparison, averages just 8.5 hours. On the surface, that looks like a serious handicap for EV adoption. Look more carefully, though, and it tells a different story.

The report, drawn from Africa E-Mobility Week held in Addis Ababa in October 2025, argues that the continent's e-mobility transition has moved well past the question of whether electric vehicles can work in African conditions. The question now is how fast the transition can scale, and which markets are positioned to lead it.

The grid as a forcing function

South Africa's load shedding years have driven rooftop solar installations and battery storage adoption at a pace few other markets can match.

The result is a growing base of energy-independent households and businesses that are, in practical terms, already well suited to home EV charging. The infrastructure is being built from the bottom up, driven by necessity rather than policy.

This matters because the AfEMA report identifies integration as the defining challenge of the decade ahead. Charging infrastructure requires grid coordination. Battery deployment requires lifecycle management. Fleet electrification requires energy planning alongside vehicle procurement.

The report is clear that these are integration problems rather than technology problems, and South Africa's private sector has been solving integration problems under pressure for years.

South Africa also has more of the formal building blocks in place than most African markets. It already has a national e-mobility strategy, active fiscal incentives, and Extended Producer Responsibility frameworks covering lithium battery disposal.

It is one of only three African markets, alongside Kenya and Rwanda, to have adopted meaningful battery lifecycle regulation — a distinction the report flags as increasingly important as deployment scales.

A continental moment arriving in Cape Town

More than 150,000 EVs have been deployed across leading African markets, with over $620 million in disclosed investment flowing into the sector since 2020. Battery swap networks are scaling rapidly, with Spiro alone operating more than 1,200 stations across six countries.

That widening gap makes the next two years consequential for South Africa. The country will host Africa E-Mobility Week in Cape Town in September 2026, a signal in itself that it is regarded as a serious player in the continental conversation — a market with the institutional depth and private sector capacity to anchor the region's most significant e-mobility gathering.

The honest picture is that South Africa's grid constraints are a genuine obstacle requiring serious investment and coordination. The more interesting observation is that those same constraints have accelerated exactly the kind of distributed, integrated energy thinking that the EV transition ultimately depends on.

The country has been stress-tested in ways that others have not. That experience, if channelled well, is a foundation rather than a liability.

items.title: Affordable hybrids and EVs gain traction
items.summary: South Africa’s new energy vehicle (NEV) market is showing fresh signs of momentum as cheaper models and a widening choice of brands bring battery electric vehicles and plug in hybrids closer to the mainstream. In…
items.content_html:
South Africa’s new energy vehicle (NEV) market is showing fresh signs of momentum as cheaper models and a widening choice of brands bring battery electric vehicles and plug in hybrids closer to the mainstream.

In a recent CNBC Africa Shifting Gears discussion, Fulufhelo Mandane, Executive: Strategic Partnerships at Absa, said Chinese vehicle makers have become a major force in local sales, with Chinese brands reaching about 13.6% of the total market in April 2026 (equivalent to 6,546 units).

He explained that the shift is being reinforced by household budget pressure, which is pushing car buyers toward sharper pricing and higher specifications.

“Consumers know they’ve got options,” noted fellow panelist Thembinkosi Pantsi, vice chairperson of the National Automobile Dealerships Association (NADA).

Pantsi noted that dealerships are responding through multi franchise showrooms that carry traditional brands alongside newer Asian entrants, helping retailers sustain volumes - and jobs - during a difficult economic period.

EV entry prices pull adoption forward

Mandane linked the rise in NEV interest to improving affordability at the entry level and greater visibility of new brands. He pointed to a lower price point for a newly introduced battery electric model as a catalyst for improving EV sales.

“Just look at March, where we saw the introduction of the Geely E2 at around R340,000,” he pointed out. He added that the (similarly priced) BYD Dolphin Surf supported about 232 units sold in March 2026, a meaningful number in a market where battery electric adoption has previously been slow.

Growth in plug in hybrids is also emerging as a practical bridge for consumers still wary of charging constraints. Mandane stated that PHEV sales rose by almost 498% year-on-year, moving from 111 units to about 664 units in March. Dealers say this matches a wider pattern in which buyers still value familiar driving habits while looking for relief from volatile fuel costs.

Mandane revealed that pressure at the pumps is influencing buying decisions. “We are seeing a lot more queries going out in the sales space for new energy vehicles,” he said, adding that finance demand is starting to follow.

Policy, skills and finance set the pace

Industry participants say the next phase [of NEV adoption] will depend on whether South Africa can expand the enabling ecosystem quickly enough. That includes charging infrastructure, technical skills for servicing high voltage drivetrains, and policy certainty that supports investment.

Pantsi said the retail industry is preparing for a different operating model as NEV sales grow. “The dealer of the future is going to be different to the dealer of today,” he stated, referring to NADA’s Motoring Mavericks initiative aimed at building skills for the next generation of technicians and dealership staff.

Banks are also reviewing product design as NEVs change the cost structure of ownership. Mandane intimated that vehicle finance may increasingly need to account for complementary equipment at home and at work.

“We are exploring different ways in which we can look at supporting the industry,” he said, citing items such as charging stations and inverters as part of the ownership journey.

For now, South Africa's NEV story is being written at the intersection of price, confidence and support. As more brands deepen their dealer networks and consider local assembly, the next five years are likely to show whether the country's NEV market can move from early adoption to mass market reality.

items.title: EV Buyers Chase Calm, Not Speed
items.summary: A new global white paper from lubricants giant Castrol has revealed something that may surprise the motoring world: the single biggest draw of electric vehicles is not performance, not cost savings, and not environmental credentials.
items.content_html:
A new global white paper from lubricants giant Castrol has revealed something that may surprise the motoring world: the single biggest draw of electric vehicles is not performance, not cost savings, and not environmental credentials. It is peace and quiet.

The report, titled The Quiet Electric Car Revolution, surveyed 3,000 drivers across the United States, Germany and China, and found that tranquillity has emerged as the defining emotional benefit of EV ownership.

The quiet driving experience ranked as the number-one functional feature that prospective EV buyers are aware of, ahead of instant acceleration and automatic software updates. A remarkable 81% of EV considerers identified it as a top appeal feature, while 83% of existing owners said they were satisfied with it.

Dirk, a 58-year-old driver from Hamburg who owns a VW ID.7, put it simply: "What I like most about my EV is actually the silent driving. It's like floating. I'm past the age where everything needs to go vroom vroom vroom."

For South African drivers navigating the daily grind of urban congestion, pothole stress and long commutes, this finding carries particular resonance. The idea of a car as a sanctuary rather than a source of frustration is a compelling one.

Performance That Puts Drivers in Control

Beyond the calm, the research found that EV drivers feel a heightened sense of control behind the wheel. A full 84% of owners said they enjoy the feeling of agile cornering and responsive handling, while 78% believe the EV driving experience is superior to that of petrol, diesel or hybrid vehicles.

Elaine Borseth, President of the EV Association of the US, described it well: "The power, the acceleration, the smoothness, the quietness. It's a superior driving experience. It's different and so much better."

Importantly, drivers are not looking for technology to replace their control. They want it to enhance it. The research found that 80% of respondents agree their car is one of the few places where they feel completely in control, and smart driver-assist features are valued precisely because they support that feeling rather than undermine it.

More Than a Car

The Castrol study also found that EVs are increasingly seen as expressions of identity. Some 74% of respondents said their car is an important part of who they are, and 44% said their vehicle reflects their passion for new technology.

EVs are now associated with being future-proof by 74% of respondents, a figure that leaves hybrids at 50% and traditional ICE vehicles trailing at just 34%.

Inside the cabin, the picture is equally compelling. With no engine taking up space, EV interiors offer more room, better design and features such as ambient lighting and massage seats. Some 83% of EV owners report satisfaction with cabin comfort, and 73% view their car as a multipurpose space for work, entertainment and relaxation.

The road ahead for EV's still has its challenges. Range anxiety, charging infrastructure and upfront costs remain real barriers. But if Castrol's research tells us anything, it is that the emotional case for going electric is already being won, one quiet, gliding journey at a time.

items.title: Lexus reveals TZ electric SUV
items.summary: Lexus has unveiled the all new TZ, a battery electric three row SUV that the company says is being evaluated for possible introduction to the South African market. Shown globally for the first time, the…
items.content_html:
Lexus has unveiled the all new TZ, a battery electric three row SUV that the company says is being evaluated for possible introduction to the South African market.

Shown globally for the first time, the TZ introduces Lexus’s new Discover Limitless philosophy and a cabin concept it calls the Driving Lounge. The brand is positioning the model as a premium, lounge-like space designed to keep all occupants relaxed and connected, with a focus on refinement and long distance comfort.

Lexus says a newly developed dedicated BEV platform contributes to a more open interior layout, supported by a wide panoramic roof and a minimalist design approach.

The company also claims high levels of cabin quietness, backed by sound management, ambient lighting and premium audio technology intended to create a calmer travel environment.

Performance, charging and practical packaging

Despite its comfort focus, Lexus is pitching the TZ as a strong performer. It uses a dual motor all wheel drive system producing 300 kW, with a claimed 0 to 100 km per hour time of 5.4 seconds.

Charging capability includes rapid DC charging, with a 10 per cent to 80 per cent charge achievable in around 35 minutes. Lexus quotes an estimated driving range of up to 640 km, depending on market specifications.

In size, the TZ measures 5,100 mm in length with a 3,050 mm wheelbase. Cargo capacity ranges from 290 litres to 2,017 litres, while towing capacity is rated at up to 1,500 kg on the EU specification.

Design direction and sustainability cues

The TZ also signals a new design direction for the brand, with a sculpted spindle body, geometric lighting elements and aerodynamic detailing aimed at improving efficiency and range. Lexus says the TZ delivers class leading aerodynamic performance among its SUV line-up.

Inside, the company highlights Forged Bamboo trim crafted from Shikoku bamboo, alongside recycled aluminium and other sustainable materials. Lexus says it has also adopted lower impact manufacturing processes as part of a circular vehicle development strategy.

Lexus cautions that the specifications released are prototype values for a pre production vehicle, with final figures expected to vary by market and grade. Further details on timing will follow should the TZ be confirmed for South Africa.

items.title: Geely Introduces E5 Apex Plus EV
items.summary: Geely Auto South Africa has expanded its electric vehicle (EV) line-up in South Africa with the introduction of the E5 Apex Plus, a midsize electric SUV priced from R788,888. The new model forms part of…
items.content_html:
Geely Auto South Africa has expanded its electric vehicle (EV) line-up in South Africa with the introduction of the E5 Apex Plus, a midsize electric SUV priced from R788,888.

The new model forms part of a three-variant range that includes the E5 Aspire from R699,999 and the E5 Apex from R759,999.

The Apex Plus sits at the top of the range and is positioned as a longer range option for buyers seeking added convenience for daily use and extended travel. It competes against rivals like the (considerably cheaper) Dongfeng Nammi 06, among others.

Range and performance specifications

The E5 Apex Plus is powered by a front mounted electric motor delivering 160 kW and 320 Nm, enabling a 0 to 100 km per hour sprint in 7.6 seconds and a top speed of 175 km per hour.

Geely has paired this with a 68.39 kWh lithium iron phosphate battery, which provides a claimed WLTP driving range of up to 450 km.

Charging capability includes AC charging up to 11 kW and DC fast charging up to 100 kW. Under fast charging conditions, the battery can be replenished from 30 per cent to 80 per cent in about 20 minutes, supporting both urban commuting and longer distance travel.

The E5’s dimensions place it firmly in the midsize SUV segment, with a length of 4,615 mm and a wheelbase of 2,750 mm. Luggage capacity is rated at 461 litres, while the flat floor design associated with electric platforms contributes to cabin space and passenger comfort.

Inside, the Apex Plus features a 15.4 inch touchscreen infotainment system and a 10.2 inch digital driver display. Other standard equipment includes wireless smartphone charging, multiple USB ports, keyless entry, voice control and over the air software updates.

Leather appointed seats, power adjustable front seats and a panoramic sunroof underline its premium positioning.

Safety and ownership support

Safety features include adaptive cruise control, autonomous emergency braking, lane keeping assist, blind spot detection and rear cross traffic alert. A driver monitoring system and multiple airbags are also standard, alongside electronic stability control and hill descent control.

Geely has sought to strengthen the ownership proposition with a comprehensive aftersales package. This includes a six year or 150,000 km vehicle warranty, a six year or 120,000 km service plan and an eight year or 200,000 km battery warranty.

Buyers also receive a wall box charger, an emergency charging cable and a R12,000 charging voucher when financing through Geely Finance.

The company says the E5 Apex Plus is aimed at South African motorists looking to transition to electric mobility with lower running costs and reduced maintenance requirements.

With its combination of range, specification and pricing, the model represents Geely’s latest push into a rapidly developing local BEV market.

items.title: EVs and the fuel levy question
items.summary: South Africa's roads are funded largely through the fuel levy — a tax built into the price of every litre of petrol or diesel sold. The more fuel you buy, the more you contribute. It…
items.content_html:
South Africa's roads are funded largely through the fuel levy — a tax built into the price of every litre of petrol or diesel sold. The more fuel you buy, the more you contribute. It is a simple system, and for decades it has worked reasonably well.

But battery electric vehicles (BEVs) do not use these fuels. They charge from the grid, and in doing so, they avoid the fuel levy entirely. As more South Africans switch to BEVs, the amount collected through the fuel levy will shrink — even though the roads those BEVs drive on still need to be built, maintained and repaired.

This is the funding gap that transport planners and economists are increasingly worried about.

Fuel levy figures tell the story

The general fuel levy has been rising steadily.

From June 2025, it stood at R4.01 per litre for petrol and R3.85 per litre for diesel. By April 2026, those figures had increased further to R4.29 per litre for petrol and R4.16 cents per litre for diesel. The Road Accident Fund levy, which funds compensation for road crash victims, also rose to R2.25 per litre.

A petrol car filling up a 50-litre tank is therefore contributing well over R300 in levies alone, every single time. An EV owner filling the same journey pays none of that.

Why a road-use charge makes sense

The idea behind a road-use charge is straightforward.

Instead of taxing the fuel a vehicle burns, the government would charge drivers based on how far they travel. The more kilometres you drive, the more you pay. It does not matter whether your vehicle runs on petrol, diesel, hydrogen or electricity — if you use the road, you contribute to its upkeep.

This also addresses a quieter problem that already exists. A fuel-efficient petrol car consuming six litres per 100 km pays far less in fuel levy per kilometre than an older car consuming 11 litres per 100 km. Both vehicles cause similar wear on the road surface, yet one contributes significantly less to road funding. A per-kilometre charge would treat them the same.

How it could work in practice

There are a few ways a road-use charge could be collected.

The simplest approach would be an odometer reading taken at licensing or roadworthy time each year*. You declare your kilometres, and a charge is calculated accordingly. It is easy to administer and raises few privacy concerns.

A more sophisticated approach would use telematics or GPS tracking. This would allow charges to vary depending on the type of road used, the time of day, traffic conditions and even the weight of the vehicle. A Western Cape pilot concept has already explored this idea, using route-based pricing to show how detailed such a system could become.

The third option is a flat annual fee added to vehicle licence renewal. This is the easiest to implement, but it treats a driver covering 5 000 km a year the same as one covering 50 000 km — which many would consider unfair.

What this means for EV owners

Lower running costs remain one of the strongest arguments for going electric, and that is unlikely to change. A road-use charge, if introduced, would add a new line to the ownership cost — but it would apply to all vehicles, not just BEVs.

The important thing for BEV owners is to follow the debate closely, keep track of annual mileage, and engage when draft proposals are published. The details — how privacy is protected, how rural drivers are treated, how the system is administered — will matter enormously.

How South Africa funds its roads in an electric future is one that government, industry and the public will need to answer together.

*A few issues are worth noting. Firstly, South Africa currently does not require annual roadworthy testing. Secondly, using odometer readings will likely increase the likelihood of "mileage manipulation", especially on older vehicles - Ed.
